newsitem.title: UK: Up to 20 hurt in bomb attack on British base.
newsitem.headline: Up to 20 hurt in bomb attack on British base.

text.p: Suspected Irish Republican guerrillas bombed Britain's Northern Ireland army headquarters on Monday, injuring up to 20 people and blowing holes in an uneasy two-year peace.

The British army, deployed 27 years ago to keep feuding Protestant and Catholic gunmen apart, has not been attacked since 1994 when rival Irish Republican Army (IRA) and Loyalist guerrillas declared truces which launched a peace process.
Hospital spokesmen said they were treating seven people but were ready to receive up to 20 victims of two explosions inside the British army base at Lisburn, south of Belfast.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack but pro-British Protestant spokesmen accused Irish Republicans fighting to end British rule.

It was the most serious attack in Northern Ireland for months and raised fears among police and politicians of a backlash by Protestant "Loyalist" guerrillas against the Catholic community from which Irish republicans draw support.
"This is obviously a Republican attack from whatever quarter," said Gary McMichael of the Ulster Democratic Party.

British Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew told the BBC from a U.S. conference: "This attack will do nothing but bring catastrophe if Loyalist paramilitaries go back to violence and I appeal to them to hold to their discipline."
There was speculation in the security forces that the explosions were caused by mortar bombs, a favoured weapon of Irish Republican guerrillas.
But army sources said it may have been a car bomb driven inside the top-security barracks where hundreds of Britain's soldiers in an 18,000-strong force are lodged.
"We have had two explosions. There was one followed 20 minutes later by a second one. We have had some casualties. Five are serious casualties," said an army officer.
"There were 20 not so serious. The second bomb exploded as casualties moved to the medical centre. They were both high explosives," the officer told Reuters.

Reverend Brian Gibson, who lives next door to the barracks, said: "I was sitting in my study when it went off. I could see shrapnel all over the playing field. It seemed to be in the middle of a field where some girls were playing hockey.
"There was no screaming, just an awful silence for a considerable length of time. Then all the emergency services started to arrive," he said.

The attack was mounted as jailed Loyalists in the top-security Maze prison met to discuss whether or not their activists should continue to abide by an October 1994 ceasefire. The blast could be heard at the prison, where 1,000 people, both Republican and Loyalist, are jailed for security offences in the 27-year Northern Ireland conflict. It also coincided with this week's conference by the ruling Conservative Party of John Major, whom Irish Republicans accuse of wrecking a two-year Anglo-Irish peace process.

The IRA ended its 17-month ceasefire in February this year by launching a wave of attacks on British targets and a British army base in Germany but has avoided targetting Northern Ireland, apparently for fear of Loyalist retaliation.

Police chiefs have warned that any IRA attack in the province itself would unleash a Loyalist backlash which could spread to the Irish Republic, which Loyalists accuse of backing the IRA and its Sinn Fein political wing.
